title: A practical checklist for verifying automation recovery
summary: Verify outputs, delivery and recovery evidence before calling an automation healthy.

sections.title: Define the observable result
sections.text: Start with the result a person needs: a published page, a readable report or a restorable archive. A successful process exit is useful evidence, but it does not establish that the result reached its destination. Record the input, execution time and expected output location before running the repair.
steps: Choose a small, explicit set of affected routes or records.
Record the previous error and the exact check that reproduced it.
Keep a copy of the configuration before changing it.

sections.title: Validate each boundary
sections.text: Check the producer and consumer separately. A generator can finish without writing the file expected by an upload step. A report can be valid locally while delivery fails. A page can return HTTP 200 while sending the browser into a redirect loop. Follow the same path a user or downstream task follows.
steps: Inspect the generated output rather than relying on a success message.
Follow redirects and verify the final destination.
Retest the published result after deployment has completed.

sections.title: Keep the next run honest
sections.text: Retain the evidence with a timestamp and a clearly stated scope. If only a sample was tested, name the sample instead of claiming complete coverage. Ensure an unchanged result stays quiet and a failed delivery can be retried. Keep a reversible previous version so a later regression can be investigated without guessing.
steps: Run a failure-path test as well as a success-path test.
Confirm the next scheduled execution and its delivery destination.
Separate repaired failures from unrelated findings that still need work.

title: Plan a restoration drill for your automation backups
summary: A backup is useful when its contents, limits and restoration steps have been checked.

sections.title: Write down the backup scope
sections.text: List the configuration, scripts and data included in the archive. Record exclusions such as credentials, databases or additional profiles. This prevents a portable configuration export from being mistaken for a complete machine backup. Choose a recovery objective that matches the files actually stored.
steps: Record the source profile and export method.
Keep the archive timestamp and a checksum with the backup.
Document every excluded data store that needs a separate recovery path.

sections.title: Test in an isolated destination
sections.text: Restore into a temporary environment with outgoing delivery disabled. Verify that the archive opens, required files exist and configuration can be read. Run a small local task that exercises the restored scripts. Avoid using a restoration drill to send customer messages or to overwrite the working production profile.
steps: Validate archive integrity before replacing an older verified copy.
Compare restored configuration with the expected version.
Check the result of a representative task without publishing it.

sections.title: Preserve evidence and a previous copy
sections.text: Record what the drill demonstrated and what it did not test. A checksum proves file equality, while a successful restoration test provides different evidence about usability. Keep the last verified archive until the new one has passed the required checks. Repeat the drill after significant configuration or storage changes.
steps: Keep the previous verified backup available.
Record the actual time and steps needed to restore.
Update the recovery instructions whenever the data scope changes.

title: How to define a measurable cloud-cost pilot
summary: Separate assumptions, operating costs and measured outcomes when planning a cloud-cost experiment.

sections.title: Choose a comparable baseline
sections.text: Start with a recent invoice and name the workloads included in the pilot. Record traffic, storage and service-level expectations alongside cost. Comparing two invoices without those conditions can hide changes in demand or scope. Keep the pilot narrow enough that its outcome can be explained.
steps: Identify the workload owner and the billing period.
Record operational constraints before proposing changes.
Keep the original configuration available for rollback.

sections.title: Separate the estimate from the observation
sections.text: An assumed percentage reduction is a planning input, not a prediction. Include recurring operational effort and one-time implementation costs when comparing scenarios. Consider more than one set of assumptions. A calculator can organize the arithmetic, but it does not inspect cloud accounts or validate a provider bill.
steps: Compare conservative and optimistic scenarios.
Record the source and date of each input.
Keep implementation costs distinct from monthly operating costs.

sections.title: Measure before expanding
sections.text: Run the pilot for an agreed period and compare actual cost and service behavior with the baseline. Record incidents, operator effort and changes in demand. Expand only after the owner reviews the evidence and the rollback path. The guide and linked calculator support planning; they do not promise a saving or replace a workload-specific assessment.
steps: Check that service requirements remain satisfied.
Compare like-for-like periods and explain changes in scope.
Document the measured result before approving a wider rollout.

title: Check redirects and sitemaps before a website release
summary: Use a small release checklist to catch missing pages, self-redirects and stale sitemap entries.

sections.title: Identify the published source
sections.text: A repository can contain multiple versions of a website. Confirm which directory the deployment actually publishes before fixing a route. A page in an application source folder will not appear in an artifact assembled only from a static public folder. Inspect the generated artifact as part of the release check.
steps: Record the deployed commit and artifact preparation command.
Check that each repaired URL has an output file.
Preserve the existing navigation and contact destinations.

sections.title: Follow the destination
sections.text: Check HTTP redirects and page-level refresh directives. Track every destination and stop when a URL repeats. Verify the final page contains the expected content rather than a generic error document. For retired URLs, use the intended current destination and make the relationship clear to visitors.
steps: Test trailing-slash variants when they are supported.
Confirm canonical links agree with the intended destination.
Provide a visible navigation link when automatic redirection is used.

sections.title: Keep discovery consistent
sections.text: A sitemap should describe pages intended for discovery. When an old URL becomes a noindex alias, remove its entry from the published sitemap. Keep unrelated entries intact and validate the resulting XML. Repeat the checks on the live domain after deployment, since a local artifact alone does not establish publication.
steps: Verify that the old URL no longer appears in the sitemap.
Check the replacement destination directly.
Save the deployment and live validation evidence together.

title: What to prepare for an AI workflow automation discovery
summary: Bring a concrete process, constraints and acceptance criteria to the first scoping conversation.

sections.title: Describe one real workflow
sections.text: Choose a process with a clear starting event and a recognizable result. Map the people, systems and handoffs involved. Record where delays or rework occur using examples you are authorized to share. A specific workflow gives the scoping discussion a better foundation than a broad request to automate everything.
steps: Name the input, owner and expected output.
Describe how exceptions are handled today.
Remove private customer information from sample material.

sections.title: Set operating boundaries
sections.text: Explain which actions may run automatically and which need human review. Include access constraints, data retention needs and existing approval rules. Distinguish read-only reporting from changes to external systems. These boundaries influence the integration design, testing plan and recovery procedure.
steps: List the connected systems and required permissions.
Identify irreversible actions and their approval points.
Define what the automation should do when a dependency is unavailable.

sections.title: Agree measurable acceptance criteria
sections.text: Define what a successful pilot must demonstrate before discussing expansion. Include correct outputs, delivery, exception handling and rollback. Use the current Zion services and plans pages for the present offering; the discovery process establishes the specific scope and commercial terms. This guide does not describe a prepackaged industry product.
steps: Choose representative success and failure examples.
Agree who reviews the pilot evidence.
Document the accepted scope before connecting production actions.

title: Define acceptance criteria for a data integration project
summary: Turn a request to connect systems into a testable agreement about data, ownership and recovery.

sections.title: Define the data contract
sections.text: List the records and fields that need to move, their source of truth and the receiving system. Explain how identifiers, timestamps and missing values are represented. Use a small authorized sample to expose differences early. A clear contract reduces ambiguity when the systems disagree.
steps: Name the owner of each source and destination.
Record required fields and acceptable values.
Define how duplicate or late records should be handled.

sections.title: Specify the failure behavior
sections.text: A useful integration plan covers partial failures as well as the happy path. Decide when a request may be retried and how a repeated request is recognized. Keep enough evidence to trace a record without logging credentials or unnecessary personal information. Describe how operators can reconcile an interrupted transfer.
steps: Test unavailable endpoints and rejected records.
Ensure retries do not create duplicate business actions.
Define a safe method for resuming after an interruption.

sections.title: Validate the outcome with the owner
sections.text: Compare source and destination records using agreed examples, then confirm the operational result with the team that uses the data. Document timing, coverage and known exclusions. A limited pilot can validate the design before a wider rollout. Scope, implementation work and commercial terms should be confirmed through the current discovery process.
steps: Check representative records end to end.
Record exceptions and unresolved mappings.
Keep the rollback and support responsibilities explicit.
